column2: Such is this nature; a man should live by his own understanding, not grieving or exulting, free of envy.
He ever creates the qualities perfected by the perfection of his nature, as the spider creates its threads; the qualities are to be known like threads.
Those destroyed do not return; return is not found; that which is unseen is established by inference from what is seen.
Some decide thus, others that there is return; having weighed both, one should decide as one's judgment allows.
Having loosened this firm knot of the heart, made of the splitting of the intellect, one should sit happily and not grieve, his doubts cut.
As the unclean gain purity by bathing in a full river, know this knowledge to be so for the well-learned.
One who knows the farther shore of a great river is not troubled in crossing; so are those who know the self, the isolation, the highest knowledge.
Knowing all this, a man, considering slowly by intellect the coming and going of beings, thereby gains the highest peace.
He who knows the three aims, with the light before him, is freed; seeking with the mind, joined, seeing the truth, free of eagerness.
The self cannot be seen divided in the senses, scattered here and there, hard to conquer for those who have not mastered themselves.
Knowing this, one becomes awakened; what other mark of the awakened is there? Knowing it, the wise regard their work as done.
For the learned there is no fear from that which is a very great fear for the unlearned; no one has a higher goal; where there is virtue they speak of incomparability.
What one does without prior intent, and what one has done before, he drives away; what is not dear, how can both those be dear? It brings it forth in the doer here.
See the world's afflicted people wailing, grieving over this and that; there see the skilled who do not grieve, who ever know both states.
[Bhishma said:] "As meditation is well practised, so do yogis, great sages satisfied with knowledge, their minds gone to extinction.
They do not return again, Partha, freed from the faults of rebirth, with the faults of birth exhausted, established in their own nature.
Free of the pairs, ever abiding in goodness, freed, ever resting, unattached, without dispute, bringing peace of mind.
There he should hold the mind one-pointed, joined with study, gathering the host of senses into one, sitting like a log, the sage.
He should not find sound with the ear, nor feel touch with the skin, nor know form with the eye, nor tastes with the tongue.
The knower of yoga should give up all smells by meditation; being strong, he should not desire these objects of the fivefold group.
Then the discerning one, merging the fivefold group in the mind, should collect the mind that wanders with the five senses.
The wandering, unsupported, five-doored, restless one: the steadfast should collect the mind within on the earlier path of meditation.
For the sage who collects himself, deliberation, reasoning and discernment arise as the first meditation, at the beginning.
If troubled by the mind, he should still practise concentration; the sage should not fall into disgust, but should do what is good for himself.
As heaps of dust, ashes and dung suddenly sprinkled with water do not take on moisture,
and as something oily, dry powder not moistened, takes it up gradually and slowly, so all that is absorbed.
So he should slowly soften the host of the senses and draw them in by degrees, and he will be rightly at peace.
The mind itself and the fivefold group, Bharata, having reached the earlier path of meditation, are stilled by constant yoga.
That happiness will come to him who is so restrained, not by human effort nor by any fate.
Joined with that happiness he will delight in the work of meditation; thus yogis go to that extinction free of disease."
[Yudhishthira said:] "I have heard from you tales joined with dharma, greatly wise; but I have a certain doubt, and you should tell it.
I wish to hear, Bharata, the attainment of fruit by the mutterers; what fruit is said for those who mutter, and where do the mutterers stay?
You should tell me the whole rule of muttering, sinless one; and what are the mutterers? Is it the rule of action of Sankhya and yoga?
Is this the rule of sacrifice, or what is called a thing to be muttered? Tell me all this, for I regard you as omniscient."
[Bhishma said:] "Here too they cite this ancient tale, of what once took place with Yama, Kala and a brahmana.
Renunciation itself, at the end of the Veda, turns to muttering; the peace produced by Vedic discussion rests in Brahman; these are two paths, both resorted to and not resorted to.
As it is heard, king, and as the reason will be told: here too concentration of mind and conquest of the senses are said to be the way.
Truth, tending the fire, resort to solitary places, meditation, austerity, self-control, forbearance, freedom from envy, moderate eating,
withdrawal from objects, little talk, and peace: this is the dharma of action; now hear the dharma of withdrawal.
How the action of a muttering celibate student stops: all this, as told, he should avoid, having reached a threefold path, manifest and unmanifest, without support.
Seated on a heap of kusha grass, kusha in hand, with kusha topknot, clad in bark, in the middle covered with kusha,
he should bow to the objects of sense and not dwell on the objects, producing equanimity of mind, setting the mind in mind.
With that thought he meditates on Brahman, muttering the beneficial Samhita, or, abiding in concentration, he renounces it.
Here meditation arises from the strength of the Samhita; with purified self, self-controlled by austerity, free of hate and desire,
free of passion and delusion, beyond the pairs, he does not grieve or cling; he stands as one with no things to be done or not to be done.
He should never set his mind in union with ego, nor be intent on grasping the self, nor scornful, nor inactive.
Intent on the practice of meditation, a meditator, resolved on meditation, having produced concentration in meditation, he gradually gives up even that.
In that state, having done all renunciation, happy, free of effort, he gives up his breaths and takes a body of Brahman.
Or, if he does not wish for the body of Brahman, he departs, standing on the path, and is not born anywhere.
Resorting to the intellect of the self, becoming calm and free of disease, he attains the self, immortal, stainless, pure."
[Bhishma said:] "Hear attentively, king, lord, the fate of the mutterers, how they go to many hells, bull among men.
The mutterer who does not follow what was told before, and performs only part of the rite here, goes to hell.
Whoever acts with contempt, is not pleased and does not grieve, such a mutterer goes to hell; there is no doubt.
All who act from ego go to hell; a man who despises others becomes one bound for hell.
He who, deluded, does his muttering with covetousness goes to whatever hell he covets.
If a mutterer, set on lordship, takes pleasure in it, that is his hell; he is not freed from it.
A mutterer who mutters with attachment, deluded, is born wherever his attachment falls.
The ill-minded, of untrained wisdom, who stays in an unsteady mind, goes to an unsteady course or reaches hell.
Many hells are listed from poor wisdom; muttering is praised, and these faults belong to it."
[Bhishma said:] "Here too they cite this ancient tale, of what took place between Ikshvaku, son of the Sun, and a brahmana,
and Time and Death; learn from me how their dialogue came about and in what place.
There was a brahmana mutterer, famed, living by dharma, versed in the six limbs, greatly wise, Paippaladi of the Kaushika line.
He had direct knowledge of the six limbs and was skilled in the Vedas, dwelling at the foot of the Himalaya.
He performed imperishable Brahmic austerity, restrained, muttering the Samhita; for a thousand years he continued so by rule.
Then the goddess showed herself to him in person, saying, "I am pleased"; he, repeating his mutterings, was silent and said nothing to her.
Out of compassion for him the goddess was pleased then; Mother of the Veda, she honoured his muttering.
When the muttering was done, the righteous one rose and fell with his head at the goddess's feet, and said these words:
By good fortune, goddess, you are pleased and have come to my sight; if you are indeed pleased, let my mind delight in muttering.
[Savitri said:] "What do you wish, brahmana sage, what desire shall I fulfil? Say, best of mutterers; all that will be yours."
Thus addressed by the goddess, the brahmana, knower of dharma, said: "I wish for my muttering, again and again, to grow.
Let my concentration of mind grow day by day, auspicious one." "So be it," the goddess then answered sweetly.
And the goddess, wishing to please him, said this also: "You will not go to hell, where the best of the twice-born have gone.
You will go to the seat of Brahma, causeless and blameless; and what you have asked of me here will be accomplished.
Restrained, mutter with one-pointed mind; dharma will come to you; Time, Death and Yama will come near you; and there will be a dispute between you and them, by dharma."
Having spoken thus, the goddess went to her own dwelling; the brahmana too stayed muttering for a divine hundred years.
When that rule was complete, Dharma himself, pleased with the wise brahmana, showed himself to him.
[Dharma said:] "Twice-born, see me, Dharma; I have come to see you. Hear also the fruit of your muttering which you have obtained.
All the worlds, divine and human, have been conquered by you; leaving behind all the hells of the gods, good one, you will go.
Give up your life-breath, sage, and go to the worlds you desire; leaving your body, you will gain the worlds."
[The brahmana said:] "I have done with the worlds, Dharma; go as you please; I will not cast off this body of many pains and pleasures, lord."
[Dharma said:] "Surely, sir, your body must be given up, bull among sages; ascend to heaven, brahmana; what do you wish, sinless one?"
[The brahmana said:] "I do not wish to dwell in heaven without my body, lord; go, Dharma; I have no desire to go to heaven without myself."
[Dharma said:] "Enough of fixing your mind on the body; give up the body and be happy; go to the stainless worlds, having gone to which one does not grieve."
[The brahmana said:] "I delight in muttering, great one; I have done with the eternal worlds; I must go to heaven with my body, or not at all."
[Dharma said:] "If you do not wish to give up the body, look: here Time, Death and Yama have come to you."
[Bhishma said:] Then Vaivasvata, Time and Death, the three, lord, came to that blessed brahmana and spoke thus:

The fruit of your well-performed austerity and good conduct is the best for you; I am Yama and I speak to you.
mahabharata:12:192.30	You have obtained the supreme fruit of this muttering in due measure; it is time for you to ascend to heaven; I am Time and have come to you.
mahabharata:12:192.31	Know me as Death, knower of rule and dharma, come in person in form, urged by Time, to lead you from here today, brahmana.
[The brahmana said:] "Welcome to the son of the Sun, and to Time the great-souled, and to Death and Dharma; what can I do for you?"
[Bhishma said:] Having offered them water for the feet and arghya, he said in that gathering, greatly pleased: "What can I do for you, as I am able?"
At that very time, Ikshvaku, who had come on a pilgrimage, reached the place where they were gathered, lord.
The royal sage, having honoured and saluted them all, the best of kings asked after the well-being of everyone.
Giving him a seat, water for feet and arghya, the brahmana, having asked after his welfare, said:
Welcome to you, great king; say whatever you wish here; what can I do for you here as I am able? Tell me.
[The king said:] "I am a king and you are a brahmana; if you are devoted to your work, I give wealth; say what you desire."
[The brahmana said:] "Brahmanas are of two kinds, king, and dharma is said to be of two kinds: of action and of withdrawal; I am withdrawn from receiving gifts.
Give gifts to those engaged in action, lord of men; I do not receive; what do you wish, what shall I give you? Tell me, best of kings; what can I accomplish by austerity?"
[The king said:] "I am a kshatriya; I never know the word 'give'; 'give battle' is what I say, best of the twice-born."
[The brahmana said:] "You are content with your own dharma, and we are content so, king; there is no reply between us to each other; do what you wish."
[The king said:] "You said before, 'I give as I am able'; I beg of you, brahmana, as my own, the fruit of this muttering."
[The brahmana said:] "You boast that battle is your constant speech and begging; yet there is no battle with me; why do you beg again?"
[The king said:] "Brahmanas are said to have speech as their thunderbolt, kshatriyas live by the strength of their arms; this is a battle of words, fierce, brahmana, between me and you."
[The brahmana said:] "My promise stands even today; what shall be given according to my ability? Say, king of kings, I shall give as my means allow; do not delay."
[The king said:] "The fruit you obtained by muttering fully for a hundred years: give it to me, if you are willing to give."
[The brahmana said:] "Take the best of the fruit of what I have muttered; take half of its fruit without hesitation.
Or, king, take all the fruit of my muttering here, if you wish all."
[The king said:] "Let it all be yours, good luck to you, the muttering I have asked for; farewell, I shall go; but tell me, what is its fruit?"
[The brahmana said:] "I do not know the fruit of what I have given, what I muttered; this Dharma, Time, Yama and Death are witnesses."
[The king said:] "What will the fruit of this unknown dharma do for me? Let the brahmana have that fruit; I do not wish it with doubt."
[The brahmana said:] "I do not take back what was given by word; my word, royal sage, is the authority for me and for you.
I never made an intention in my muttering; how, tiger among kings, can I know the fruit of the muttering?
You said 'give,' and I said 'I give'; I shall not spoil my word; keep truth, be firm.
If you do not do as I say today, there will be great adharma for you, king, a falsehood made.
It is not fit for you to speak falsely, scourge of foes; and neither can I speak a greater falsehood.
I promised before, without deliberation, 'I give'; take it without deliberation, if you stand in truth.
Coming here, king, you asked me for the fruit of my muttering; take what is given by me, and be firm in truth.
This world is not for one given to lies, nor the next; he cannot save his forebears, how then his descendants, king?
Neither sacrifice, study, giving nor rules carry one across in the other world as truth does, bull among men.
The austerities that have been practised and the austerity you will practise for hundreds and thousands of years do not exceed truth.
Truth is the one-syllabled Brahman, truth the one-syllabled austerity, truth the one-syllabled sacrifice, truth the one-syllabled scripture.
Truth is awake in the Vedas; the supreme fruit is said to be in truth; from truth come dharma and self-control; all is established in truth.
Truth is the Vedas and their limbs, truth the sacrifice and its rule, truth the observance of vows, and truth is Om.
Truth is the birth of living beings, truth is progeny; by truth the wind blows, by truth the sun shines.
By truth fire burns, heaven is founded on truth; truth is sacrifice, austerity, the Vedas, the stobha chants, the mantras and Sarasvati.
We have heard that dharma and truth were put on the scales; where the scale was even, truth was the heavier.
Where there is dharma there is truth; all grows by truth; why do you wish, king, to do a deed of falsehood?
Make your mind firm in truth, king; do not do untruth; why do you make it a wicked untruth to say 'give'?
If you will not take the fruit of muttering given by me, king, you will fall from your own dharma and wander the worlds.
He who promises and does not wish to give, and he who begs and does not wish to take, both are liars; you should not make it false."
[The king said:] "Fighting and protecting are the kshatriya's dharma, brahmana; kshatriyas are said to be givers; how can I take from you?"
[The brahmana said:] "I do not entice you, king, nor have I come to your house; having come here and begged, how is it you do not take?"
[Dharma said:] "Let there be no dispute between you; the wealth has come to me, Dharma. Let the brahmana be joined with the fruit of giving, and the king with the fruit of truth."
[Heaven said:] "Know me, king, as Heaven, come in person in form; let there be no dispute between you; you two are of equal fruit."
[The king said:] "I have no business with Heaven; go, Heaven, as you please; if the brahmana wishes to give, let him give and let him take my wealth."
[The brahmana said:] "If in childhood, through ignorance, I held out my hand, I now practise the dharma marked by withdrawal, muttering the Samhita.
How do you tempt me, king, a brahmana long withdrawn? I shall act by my own means; I do not want fruit from you; I am given to austerity and study and withdrawn from taking."
[The king said:] "If, brahmana, the highest fruit of your muttering has been given up by you, let whatever fruit there is of us both be shared between us here.
Brahmanas are engaged in taking, kings are givers; if dharma has been heard, brahmana, let the fruit be ours together.
Or if it is not to be shared between us, take my fruit; accept the dharma done by me, if you have favour for me."
[Bhishma said:] Then two men of deformed behaviour appeared, seizing and clasping each other, in ragged clothes, and said:
You do not owe me, said one; "I owe you," said the other; "this is our dispute; this king is the ruler."
I tell the truth: you do not owe me; you tell a falsehood here; I owe you a debt.
Both, greatly distressed, said to the king, "Let it be examined so that we are not reviled here."
[Vikrita said:] "I owe, tiger among men, the fruit of the cow of Vikrita here; and Vikrita does not take it from me when I offer it, lord of the earth."
[Virupa said:] "This Virupa does not owe me anything, lord of men; he speaks falsely; he speaks falsely to you."
[The king said:] "Virupa, what do you owe him? Tell me; having heard, I shall decide; so my mind is set."
[Virupa said:] "Hear attentively, king, how I owe this Vikrita, all of it, bull among men.
Long ago, sinless one, he gave a good cow to a brahmana devoted to austerity and study, to acquire dharma, royal sage.
And I, king, approached him and asked for the fruit of that; and Vikrita gave it to me with a pure heart.
Then I did a good deed for the purification of myself: I bought two tawny cows, calf-bearing, of much milk.
And I gave them, king, to a gleaner for his livelihood, by rule and with faith; of that I again owe to him, lord.
Taking it here today I would pay him back double the fruit of one cow; tiger among men, who is pure here and who at fault?
Disputing thus, we two have come to you here, king; do dharma or adharma; settle us by right procedure.
If he does not wish to take my gift as given by him, then, lord, remain firm here and set us on the road."
[The king said:] "Why do you not take the debt that is offered? Take it as it was permitted to you, and do not delay."
[Vikrita said:] "He said 'let it be given,' and I said 'I give'; he owes me nothing here; let him go where he wishes."
[The king said:] "You do not take what he gives; this seems unfair to me; you are to be fined by me, without doubt."
[Vikrita said:] "It was given by me to him, royal sage; how can I take it back? Let the fault be mine; order the fine, lord."
[Virupa said:] "If you will not take it as I give it, in any way, this king, the ruler of dharma, will restrain you."
[Vikrita said:] "My own was given by me when asked; how can I take it back today? Go; I give you leave."
[The brahmana said:] "You have heard this, king, said by these two; take what I promised you without deliberation."
[The king said:] "A great matter has been set before us, as if a chasm; how shall the firmness of the mutterer be?
If I do not take what the brahmana has given up, how shall I not be stained today by great fault?"
[Bhishma said:] The royal sage said to those two, "You have done your work; you may go. Now having come to me, the dharma of kings cannot be false.
The dharma of kings is to be kept; this is the settled rule; and the brahmana's dharma, heavy indeed, has entered me, who am not master of myself."
[The brahmana said:] "Take it; I hold it for you; I have heard what you asked; if you do not take it, king, I shall curse you; there is no doubt."
[The king said:] "Shame on the dharma of kings, whose settlement of this matter is such; thus I must take it; how can it be equal?
This hand, never before outstretched, is held out for a deposit; whatever you hold for me, brahmana, give it now."
[The brahmana said:] "Whatever merit I have made by muttering the Samhita, take it all, if there is anything of mine here."
[The king said:] "This water has fallen in my hand, best of the twice-born; let it be equal, let it be together; let you also receive."
[Virupa said:] "Know us as Desire and Anger; you were made to act by us two; and what you said, 'equal,' the worlds are equal for you and for him.
He holds nothing; the test was made for you; Time, Dharma, Death, Desire and Anger, and the two of you.
All has been rubbed out in mutual friction before your eyes; go to the worlds won by your own deed, wherever you wish."
[Bhishma said:] "The attainment of fruit by mutterers has been told to you by me, and their goal, their place and the worlds as conquered by a mutterer.
The student of the Samhita goes to Brahma, the supreme lord, or comes to fire, or enters the sun.
If there, in that radiant state, he takes delight, he takes up their qualities, deluded by attachment.
So in the moon and the wind, with body of earth or space, attached he dwells there practising their qualities.
Then, if he is free of attachment there, he goes to the highest doubt; wishing the supreme imperishable, he enters that very one again.
Gained from the immortal to the immortal, become cool, selfless, become Brahman, beyond the pairs, happy, calm, free of disease,
he reaches the seat of Brahman, from which there is no return, the one called the imperishable, free of sorrow, undecaying and calm.
Having passed beyond the Person, devoid of four marks, six, and sixteen, he reaches space.
Or if he wishes, with an attached self, he governs all of it, and whatever he prays for he reaches by mind.
Or he looks on all the worlds established in hell, free of desire, freed on every side, and delights happy in that very place.
Thus, great king, is the goal of the mutterer; all this has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?"
[Yudhishthira said:] "But what did those two do, if they went there as you have told, or what was the dialogue between them?"
[Bhishma said:] "Saying 'so be it,' and honouring Dharma, Yama, Time, Death and Heaven, who were worthy,
and the others, the best of brahmanas who had gathered there before, honouring all with his head, he spoke to the king:
'Joined with this fruit, royal sage, go to merit; permitted by you, I shall mutter again.
And a boon was given to me before by the goddess, mighty one, that I would ever have faith in muttering, lord of the people.'
[The king said:] 'If the success is thus fruitless, and you have faith in muttering, go, brahmana; with me gain the fruit of the mutterer.'
[The brahmana said:] 'Great effort has been made in the presence of all here; let us two go with equal fruit to where our goal is.'
[Bhishma said:] Knowing the resolve of those two, the lord of the thirty gods came with the gods and with the guardians of the world.
The gandharva Chitrasena with his retinue, the nagas, perfected ones and sages, the god of gods Prajapati, and Vishnu of a thousand heads, the inconceivable god, came.
Drums and trumpets sounded in the sky, lord, and divine showers of flowers fell there on those great souls; groups of apsarases danced there on every side.
Then Heaven in his form said to the brahmana, 'You are perfected, great one, and you, king, are perfected.'
Then the two together, king, by rule and with each other, both performed the withdrawal from objects.
Prana, apana, udana, samana and vyana: so placing them in the mind, they set the mind on the life-breaths.
Fixing at the tip of the nose, below the brows, at the saffron-place, they slowly held it with the mind.
With motionless bodies, steady in gaze, collected, having mastered their posture, they placed the self in the head.
Marutta's son was a king named Dyutiman, greatly fortunate, of great splendour, of great strength and great might.
Likewise two sons of Angiras, equal in vow, Brihaspati of great splendour and Samvarta rich in austerity, were there.
What is kingdom or enjoyment, or sacrifices, or happiness to me, for whom you, lord of the earth, have met these sorrows?
And the grass too was seen to turn into clubs; know, lord of the earth, that it was all made by Brahma's rod.
Then Dharma and Shakra and the Maruts and the Ashvins, the gods and divine sages, placed the Pandava in a chariot.
Then Shakra, lord of the gods, joined with the highest splendour, spoke to Yudhishthira these words, preceded by gentle address.
